title: Question 5
stem:
Part of an electric circuit is shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

The circuit is used to produce half-wave rectification of an alternating voltage of potential difference (p.d.) $V_{IN}$.

The output p.d. across the $14\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor is $V_{OUT}$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text:
A component is missing from the circuit of Fig. 5.1.

Complete the circuit diagram in Fig. 5.1 by adding the circuit symbol for the missing component, correctly connected.

markscheme_points.text: correct circuit symbol for a diode shown correctly co

hints: Hint 1: Think about what type of component is needed to turn a.c. into half-wave rectified current by blocking one half-cycle and passing the other.
parts.proper_answer: A diode connected in series in the top lead, with forward direction from left to right (anode to $V_{IN}$, cathode toward $V_{OUT}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what half-wave rectification needs**
You are sitting with a circuit that must pass current only half the time. That means you need a one-way valve for charge. A diode conducts with very low resistance in the forward direction and blocks current in the reverse direction.

Step 2: **Place and orient the diode**
Put the diode symbol - triangle pointing to a bar - in the dashed box in series. Since Fig. 5.3 shows positive $V_{OUT}$ when $V_{IN}$ is positive, the forward direction must be left to right, so the triangle (anode) is on the left and the bar (cathode) is on the right.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
A capacitor C is shown in the circuit of Fig. 5.1.

State the effect on $V_{OUT}$ of including the capacitor in the circuit.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the capacitor does when the diode stops conducting - where does the resistor get its current from?
parts.proper_answer: $V_{OUT}$ is smoothed - the capacitor reduces the variation / ripple in $V_{OUT}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See the capacitor as a reservoir**
Without the capacitor, $V_{OUT}$ would fall to zero whenever the diode blocks. With the capacitor in parallel with the resistor, it charges up when the diode conducts and then stores that charge.

Step 2: **Link to smoothing**
When the diode is off, the capacitor discharges slowly through the $14\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor, keeping $V_{OUT}$ up. So the sharp on-off rectified waveform is smoothed into a slowly varying d.c. voltage.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.2 and find the time for one complete repeat of the $V_{IN}$ pattern, from the start of one positive pulse to the start of the next.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period from Fig. 5.2**
The positive pulse starts at $t = 0$ and the next identical positive pulse starts at $t = 0.040\text{ s}$. So one full cycle takes: $$T = 0.040\text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Convert period to frequency**
Frequency is the number of cycles per second: $$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{0.040} = 25\text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the time constant $\tau$ for the discharge of the capacitor through the resistor is $0.038\text{ s}$.

markscheme_points.text: $V = V_{0} \exp(-t / RC)$ and $\tau = RC$ or $V = V_{0} \exp(-t / \tau)$

hints: Hint 1: Identify the discharge section in Fig. 5.3 where the diode is off - note the starting voltage $V_0$ at $t = 0.02\text{ s}$ and the voltage after $0.020\text{ s}$ of discharge.
Hint 2: Recall the exponential discharge law with time constant $\tau = RC$ and rearrange it with logarithms to solve for $\tau$.
parts.proper_answer: Using $V = V_0 \exp(-t/\tau)$ with $V_0 = 5.50\text{ V}$, $V = 3.25\text{ V}$ at $t = 0.020\text{ s}$ gives $\tau = 0.038\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick out the discharge data**
In Fig. 5.3 the capacitor charges to about $V_0 = 5.50\text{ V}$ and holds it until $t = 0.020\text{ s}$. Then $V_{IN}$ goes negative, the diode blocks, and the capacitor discharges through the resistor. After discharge time $t = 0.020\text{ s}$ (at $t = 0.040\text{ s}$) the voltage has fallen to $V = 3.25\text{ V}$.

Step 2: **Apply the discharge equation**
For discharge through resistance $R$: $$V = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{RC}\right) = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right)$$ where $\tau = RC$. Substitute the values: $$3.25 = 5.50 \exp\left(-\frac{0.020}{\tau}\right)$$

Step 3: **Solve for the time constant**
Rearrange: $$\frac{3.25}{5.50} = \exp\left(-\frac{0.020}{\tau}\right)$$ Take natural log: $$\ln\left(\frac{3.25}{5.50}\right) = -\frac{0.020}{\tau}$$ This gives $\tau \approx 0.038\text{ s}$, as required.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance of C. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: Remember the link between time constant, resistance and capacitance for a discharging capacitor.
Hint 2: Check the resistor value is in ohms ($14\text{ k}\Omega = 14000\,\Omega$) before dividing to get capacitance in farads.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the time constant relation**
The discharge time constant is set by $R$ and $C$ together: $$\tau = RC$$ So capacitance is: $$C = \frac{\tau}{R}$$

Step 2: **Insert numbers with correct units**
$\tau = 0.038\text{ s}$ and $R = 14\text{ k}\Omega = 14000\,\Omega$: $$C = \frac{0.038}{14000} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$$ That is about $2.7\,\mu\text{F}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The circuit of Fig. 5.1 is modified so that it produces full-wave rectification of an input voltage.

Suggest, with a reason, how $V_{OUT}$ now varies with time when $V_{IN}$ is as shown in Fig. 5.2.

markscheme_points.text: $V_{IN}$ has constant magnitude in both positive and neg
(so) $V_{OUT}$ is (now) constant / $V_{OUT}$ does not vary with

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.2 - what is special about the size of $V_{IN}$ in the negative half-cycle compared to the positive half-cycle?
Hint 2: Think about what full-wave rectification does to a negative voltage, and whether the capacitor will then get a chance to discharge.
parts.proper_answer: $V_{IN}$ in Fig. 5.2 has constant magnitude ($5.5\text{ V}$) in both positive and negative half-cycles, so after full-wave rectification the capacitor is always recharged and $V_{OUT}$ remains constant (at about $5.5\text{ V}$) with no discharge decay.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare half-wave and full-wave**
In half-wave, the negative half-cycle is blocked, leaving a $0.020\text{ s}$ gap where the capacitor must discharge, as seen in Fig. 5.3. In full-wave, the negative half-cycle is flipped to positive, so the diode system conducts on both halves.

Step 2: **Apply to this square wave**
Fig. 5.2 is a square wave with magnitude about $5.5\text{ V}$ whether $V_{IN}$ is positive or negative. After full-wave rectification the input to the smoothing capacitor is therefore always about $+5.5\text{ V}$. The capacitor is continuously topped up and never left to discharge, so $V_{OUT}$ stays essentially constant at the peak value and does not show the falling sections of Fig. 5.3.

enrichment.label: (c)
key_concepts: no discharge time so constant smoothed output
